tagline: A lake circuit through glacial hills, former ports and northern marshes.
intro: The Cayuga Lake Scenic Byway makes an 87-mile loop through lake views, woodland and farmland. Steep hills at the south give way to rolling fields and extensive wetlands at the north. The lake is just under 39 miles long, widening to three and a half miles near Aurora. New York’s Department of Transportation designated the circuit a State Scenic Byway in 2002. The Federal Highway Administration highlights vineyards, lakeside bluffs and sites of the women’s rights movement among its attractions.

Earlier journeys combined water and land travel: visitors to Taughannock House took a train to the lake, a steamboat across it and a stagecoach to the hotel. On the opposite shore, Aurora shipped farm produce by lake and Erie Canal. Road travel changed the western communities too: Route 96 through Trumansburg was enlarged and rerouted in 1961. As the road between Trumansburg and Ithaca improved, Trumansburg became home to faculty and staff from Cornell University and Ithaca College.

Begin at the north end and head down the western side past Canoga toward Taughannock Falls, southeast of Trumansburg. Ithaca marks the lake’s southern end. Turn north along the eastern side through King Ferry, Aurora and Union Springs, then Cayuga at the northeast end.

moments.title: Taughannock Falls State Park
moments.text: Taughannock Falls drops 215 feet where a stream-cut valley meets the deeper valley carved by glaciers for Cayuga Lake. Water wears away shale below harder siltstone and sandstone, gradually extending the gorge westward. Freezing and thawing widen small faults in the rock, allowing large sections to break away and enlarge the gorge. The falls drew nineteenth-century tourists arriving by train, steamboat and stagecoach. In 1925, as the hotels declined, New York began buying land for a state park. The former Taughannock House hotel site now holds the park’s visitor center and parking lot, while cliffs along the gorge reach 400 feet.
moments.notice: The main waterfall plunges 215 feet within a gorge whose cliffs rise as high as 400 feet.

moments.title: Aurora
moments.text: Aurora’s lakeshore served as a shipping port for the surrounding farms. After the Cayuga–Seneca Canal opened, boats carried produce up the lake and onward through the Erie Canal to larger markets. Changes in transport, the development of the Midwest and other economic shifts reduced the importance of local agriculture. Education became another part of village life: Henry Wells founded Wells College for women in 1868. The college admitted men in 2005 and closed in 2024. The village and former college share a historic district, listed on the National Register in 1980, with more than 50 contributing properties.

moments.title: Union Springs
moments.text: Frontenac Island appears as a clump of trees offshore from Union Springs. It contains a Late Archaic archaeological site dating to approximately 2000 BC, with stone tools associated with both Lamoka and Brewerton traditions. The island is ceremonially important to the Cayuga. Union Springs took ownership of the island in 1856. In 1859, nearly a third of it was removed to build an embankment for the New York Central Railroad on the eastern shore, without regard for artifacts. Later excavations recovered material for study and display at the Rochester Museum of Arts and Sciences.
moments.notice: Frontenac Island’s trees rise offshore from Union Springs.
